summary: Markets are trading with a cautious, risk-off tone as Wall Street ended lower amid fading hopes for a US-Iran diplomatic resolution, with the S&P 500 largely muted and Gulf equity markets selling off sharply on deteriorating deal prospects. The primary macro driver is the escalating US-Iran standoff, which has triggered a spike in oil prices, disrupted Strait of Hormuz shipping traffic to as few as six vessels, and prompted military incidents including the US firing on a Panama-flagged ship attempting to break an Iranian port blockade. At the sector level, industrials are under pressure as at least one major portfolio is rotating out of the space in favor of AI and memory chip plays, reflecting continued institutional conviction in the semiconductor trade following Wall Street's endorsement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's AI infrastructure vision. The dominant risk factors are geopolitical in nature — Houthi attacks in the Red Sea killing crew members, Gulf of Oman maritime incidents, elevated oil prices clouding the Federal Reserve's rate-cut calculus, and a weakening rupee signaling broader emerging market stress from energy cost pressures. In the near term, markets will remain hostage to headline risk around Iran negotiations and Hormuz shipping developments, with any credible ceasefire or diplomatic breakthrough likely triggering a sharp relief rally, while prolonged impasse keeps energy prices elevated and risk assets under pressure.
